gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what a self-hosted NAS means for a 5-person remote team in time and money. At the US median upload speed of 68.31 Mbps, one 1 GB file takes about 2 minutes to reach one remote user and about 10 minutes when all five pull it at once. A DS225+ running all day costs about $27 a year in electricity. Power plus 1 TB of Backblaze B2 offsite backup comes to about $1.84 per user per month, against $14 for Google Workspace Business Standard. That leaves about $2,190 for the NAS and its drives before three years of the NAS cost more than Workspace.
standout_why: I compared against the three pages ChatGPT cited (Synology Drive tech specs for DSM 7.4, the Drive Admin Console KB and the Drive admin Quick Start). The tech specs list version limits (32), client limits (500,000 files per client) and supported operating systems. They give no cost, bandwidth, upload speed or power figures. Both KB pages came back as empty page shells with no numbers. ChatGPT's answer used a made-up 20 Mbps upload and a $12 per-seat price that it labelled 'not verified'. Google's pricing page shows $14 for Business Standard today. Our current page already has the $2,520 three-year Workspace total. It does not have the time to move a file over a home upload line, the electricity cost, or the most a buyer can spend on hardware before Workspace becomes the cheaper option.
decides: This supports 'yes, for file storage and sync' for a 5-person team. Running costs are about an eighth of a Business Standard seat, and the DS225+ is rated for 10 Drive users, so five fit with room to spare. The real limit is the upload line where the NAS sits. At a median 68 Mbps, five people pulling large video or design files at the same time wait about 10 minutes per GB. That points large-file teams toward fiber or a high-split cable plan, or toward hosted storage. Teams that mostly share small documents are not affected.

findings.source_title: Ookla: U.S. dominates global WiFi 7 while adoption grew 4X to 7.2% by Q1-2026 (IEEE ComSoc Technology Blog)
findings.note: Ookla figure as quoted by IEEE ComSoc (Alan Weissberger, 2026-08-05). The post prints the upload number without a unit; it is read as Mbps to match the download figure.

findings.label: Time for remote users to pull a 1 GB file from a NAS on a median US upload line
findings.value: about 2 min for one user; about 9.8 min each when all 5 download at once (13.7 Mbps per user)
findings.source_title: Ookla: U.S. dominates global WiFi 7 while adoption grew 4X to 7.2% by Q1-2026 (IEEE ComSoc Technology Blog)
findings.note: 8,000 Mb ÷ 68.31 Mbps = 117 s; 5 × 117 s = 586 s ≈ 9.8 min; 68.31 ÷ 5 = 13.7 Mbps each. Ignores protocol overhead and relay hops, so real times will be longer.
